title: Diet, sugar & nutrition
blurb: Free sugars, the Stephan curve, why how often matters more than how much, hidden sugars on labels, and practical diet advice.
question: A delivery driver with several new cavities says he 'hardly has any sugar': just one spoonful in each of the eight coffees he drinks during his shift, and a bag of dried fruit he nibbles in the van. What would you explain to him, and what changes would you suggest?

teach.body: Plaque bacteria break down sugars and produce acid. The acid lowers the pH of plaque, and below the critical pH of about 5.5 enamel starts to lose mineral (demineralisation). The sugars that matter most are free sugars: sugars added to food and drink by manufacturers, cooks or consumers, plus the sugars naturally present in honey, syrups, unsweetened fruit juice and smoothies. Sugars inside whole fruit and vegetables, and the lactose naturally in plain milk, are not free sugars.

teach.h: The Stephan curve: one sugar intake
teach.caption: pH falls below 5.5 within minutes. Saliva then buffers the acid and pH slowly recovers over roughly 20 minutes to an hour, when remineralisation can happen.

teach.h: How often matters more than how much
teach.body: Every time sugar goes in, the pH drops and an acid attack begins, however small the amount. Eight coffees with one sugar each means eight acid attacks; the same sugar in one sitting means one. Frequent sipping and grazing keep the pH low for most of the day, so saliva never gets the chance to repair the enamel. The key advice is to keep sugary foods and drinks to mealtimes and cut down both the amount and the frequency.

teach.caption: Free sugars should make up no more than 5% of daily energy. Under-4s have no set limit but should avoid sugar-sweetened drinks and food with added sugar. A single can of full-sugar cola can contain more than the whole adult limit.

teach.h: Reading the label: is it a free sugar?

rows.label: Honey, syrups, agave, invert sugar, molasses
Fruit juice, smoothies, fruit juice concentrate
Sugars inside whole fruit and vegetables

teach.note: Tip: words ending in '-ose' and anything called a syrup are sugars. The higher up the ingredients list, the more there is.

head: Looks healthy
The catch
Better choice
rows: Water; juice max 150 ml a day, at a meal

teach.body: Best drinks between meals are plain water or plain milk. Safer snacks include cheese, raw vegetables and plain breadsticks. Avoid sugary foods and drinks at bedtime, when saliva flow drops. Babies' bottles should hold only breast milk, formula or cooled boiled water; introduce a free-flow cup from 6 months and discourage bottles from 1 year. For grazers and shift workers, plan meals and snacks with water in between. Use sugar-free medicines, and chewing sugar-free gum after meals boosts saliva.

Advice should fit the Eatwell Guide, so it supports general health too: high sugar intake is also linked to obesity and type 2 diabetes. Nutrition affects the mouth in other ways. Calcium, phosphate and vitamin D are needed while teeth develop, and severe vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) causes swollen, bleeding gums. Acidic drinks such as fizzy drinks and fruit juice also cause erosion, which is acid wear without bacteria, so they are doubly worth limiting.

teach.text: 'Natural' sugars still cause decay. Honey, fruit juice and smoothies are free sugars, and swapping cola for sweetened juice makes no difference if it's still sipped all day. The problem is how often sugar reaches the teeth.

items: Bacteria turn sugar into acid; below pH 5.5 enamel demineralises.
Frequency matters more than amount: every intake is an acid attack.
Keep sugar to mealtimes; water or plain milk between meals; cheese or vegetables as snacks.
Free sugars max: 30 g adults, 24 g age 7–10, 19 g age 4–6.
Spot hidden sugars: '-ose' words, syrups, honey, juice concentrate; ask for sugar-free medicines.

summary: You can now explain how sugar leads to acid attack, read the Stephan curve and the critical pH of 5.5, explain why frequency matters more than amount, define free sugars and spot hidden sugars on labels, give the UK daily sugar limits, and offer practical diet advice that fits the Eatwell Guide.

A.q: A patient has one spoonful of sugar in each of eight coffees a day. What is the main concern?
options: The total amount is very high
Sugar in hot drinks is harmless
A.why: Each sugared coffee causes a separate acid attack, so eight a day keeps the plaque pH low for much of the day.

whyNot.0: The total is modest; it's the number of intakes that does the damage.
whyNot.1: Coffee doesn't neutralise sugar; plaque bacteria still make acid.
whyNot.2: Sugar in any drink feeds plaque bacteria and causes acid.

A.q: On the Stephan curve, what is the critical pH below which enamel starts to demineralise?
A.why: Enamel begins to lose mineral when plaque pH falls below about 5.5, the critical pH.

whyNot.0: pH 7.0 is neutral; enamel is stable there.
whyNot.1: pH 6.5 is close to resting plaque pH and doesn't cause demineralisation.
whyNot.3: pH 3.0 is far below the critical point; demineralisation starts much earlier.

A.q: A patient wants the best drink to have between meals. What do you recommend?
A.why: Plain water (or plain milk) contains no free sugars or acid, so it is the safest drink between meals.

whyNot.1: Unsweetened juice still contains free sugars and acid.
whyNot.2: Sugar-free fizzy drinks are acidic and can cause erosion.
whyNot.3: Smoothies count as free sugars and are acidic.

B.q: A parent says their child snacks on sweets several times a day. What is the best advice?
options: Spread sweets evenly through the day
B.why: Reducing the number of sugar occasions, ideally to mealtimes, reduces the number of acid attacks.

whyNot.0: Spreading sweets out increases the number of acid attacks.
whyNot.2: Saliva flow drops at night, so bedtime sugar is especially harmful.
whyNot.3: Sticky sweets stay on the teeth longer, prolonging the acid attack.

B.q: Which of these is a free sugar?
B.why: Honey counts as a free sugar, along with added sugars, syrups and fruit juice.

whyNot.0: Sugars within the cell structure of whole fruit are not free sugars.
whyNot.1: Lactose naturally present in plain milk is not counted as a free sugar.
whyNot.2: Sugars inside whole vegetables are not free sugars.

B.q: A patient nibbles dried fruit throughout the working day. What is the best advice?
options: Eat it slowly to savour it
B.why: Dried fruit is sticky and high in sugar, so it should be eaten with meals rather than grazed on.

whyNot.1: Hourly snacking still means frequent sugar intakes.
whyNot.2: Eating it slowly prolongs the acid attack.
whyNot.3: Bedtime is the worst time, as saliva flow falls during sleep.

C.q: What is the recommended maximum daily free sugar intake for an adult in the UK?
C.why: Adults should have no more than 30 g of free sugars a day, roughly 7 sugar cubes.

whyNot.0: 19 g is the maximum for children aged 4 to 6.
whyNot.1: 24 g is the maximum for children aged 7 to 10.
whyNot.3: 50 g is well above the UK recommendation.

C.q: A patient swaps cola for sweetened fruit juice but still sips it all afternoon. How should this be interpreted?
options: The swap has removed the risk
C.why: Sweetened juice still contains free sugars and acid, so sipping it all afternoon still means repeated acid attacks.

whyNot.0: The frequency of sugar exposure hasn't changed, so the risk remains.
whyNot.1: Fruit juice contains free sugars and acid that can harm teeth.
whyNot.3: Fruit juice is acidic too and can also cause erosion.

C.q: Why should sugary food and drink be avoided at bedtime?
options: Sugar is absorbed faster at night
Enamel is softer in the evening
C.why: Saliva flow and its buffering capacity fall during sleep, so acid stays on the teeth for longer.

whyNot.1: Absorption speed isn't the reason; it's reduced saliva in the mouth.
whyNot.2: Night-time brushing with fluoride toothpaste is particularly valuable.
whyNot.3: Enamel hardness doesn't change with the time of day.

reteach.title: Count the attacks, not the spoonfuls
reteach.question: Two patients eat exactly the same bag of sweets each day. One eats it after lunch; the other has one sweet every half hour. Who is more at risk, and why?

blocks.h: Each sweet starts the clock again
blocks.body: After any sugar, the plaque pH dips below 5.5 for a while and then saliva slowly brings it back up. The lunchtime patient has one dip, then hours of repair time. The half-hourly patient restarts the dip every 30 minutes, so their pH never fully recovers and the enamel is under attack all afternoon. Same sugar, very different damage. That's why you always ask patients how OFTEN they have sugar, not just how much.

blocks.caption: A sweet every 30 minutes keeps knocking the pH back down before it can recover.

blocks.text: If a patient asks 'how much sugar is OK?', give the daily limit, but stress that keeping it to mealtimes matters even more.

explain.body: Free sugars are sugars added to food and drink, plus those in honey, syrups, fruit juice and smoothies. Sugars inside whole fruit, vegetables and plain milk aren't free sugars.

test.q: Which of these counts as a free sugar?
test.why: The sugars in fruit juice, even unsweetened, count as free sugars because they've been released from the fruit's cells.

whyNot.0: Lactose naturally in plain milk is not a free sugar.
whyNot.1: Sugars inside whole fruit are not free sugars.
whyNot.3: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol sweetener that plaque bacteria can't readily ferment.

explain.body: After sugar, plaque pH falls below the critical 5.5 within minutes, then saliva brings it back up over about 20 minutes to an hour. Below 5.5 enamel demineralises; above it, it can remineralise.

test.q: What happens to plaque pH in the minutes after a sugary drink?
test.why: Bacteria quickly turn sugar into acid, so plaque pH drops below the critical 5.5 within minutes.

whyNot.0: pH falls (becomes more acidic) after sugar, it doesn't rise.
whyNot.3: The drop happens within minutes of every sugar intake, at any time of day.

explain.body: Each sugar intake is an acid attack. Frequent snacking or sipping keeps pH low most of the day, so enamel can't recover. Keep sugar to mealtimes.

test.q: A shift worker grazes all day. Which plan best reduces sugar exposure?
test.why: Planned meals with water in between, and non-sugary planned snacks, cut the number of acid attacks.

whyNot.0: Hourly snacks and juice mean frequent sugar intakes.
whyNot.2: Spreading sweets out increases acid attacks.
whyNot.3: Energy drinks are usually sugary and acidic.

explain.body: Look for '-ose' words, syrups, honey and juice concentrate on labels. Dried fruit, flavoured yoghurts, cereal bars, sauces and liquid medicines often hide sugar. Safer snacks: cheese, raw vegetables, plain breadsticks.

test.q: A patient wants a tooth-friendly snack between meals. Which is best?
test.why: Cheese contains no free sugars and is a tooth-friendly snack between meals.

whyNot.0: Cereal bars often contain syrups and honey.
whyNot.1: Dried fruit is concentrated and sticky.
whyNot.3: Flavoured yoghurts usually contain added sugar.
